https://aeon.co/essays/history-and-philo.standfirst: Historian Marnie Hughes-Warrington argues that professional history loses something essential when it treats surprise, uncertainty and the strangeness of the past as embarrassments to be explained away.
body: Question: Can wonder help history and philosophy become more accurate rather than less rigorous?
Thesis: Hughes-Warrington argues that tidy professional histories can conceal the genuine strangeness of other times, and that wonder can reopen inquiry.
Argument: History is not only the sorting of records into established narratives. Encountering unfamiliar practices and categories exposes what present-day historians take for granted.
Background: Aristotle connected philosophy with wonder. Later historians prized verification but also faced traditions of strange stories, satire and paradox.
Example: A historical account that reduces an unfamiliar ritual to a modern equivalent may be readable but erase what its participants understood themselves to be doing.
Objection: An appeal to wonder can invite sensationalism, exoticism or uncritical acceptance of doubtful stories.
Response: The essay does not demand credulity; it asks historians to preserve perplexity while applying evidence and critique.
Implication: Intellectual humility may require making room for genuine surprise rather than translating everything into familiar categories.
Unresolved: How can institutions reward curiosity without sacrificing standards? What historical experiences resist our categories?
